chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Big Sid on the first bop sides; Dizzy and Bird at Billy Berg's; Camarillo
summary: Sid adapted to bop drumming; Bird broke down in Los Angeles and wrote of Camarillo.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well, Stan Levy was a real good brush man, but he didn't make the records. He was with the band, but he didn't record it. Big Sid Catlett recorded it. Now, this is something else that people aren't aware of. When you get a big band drummer, it's hard for him to tone himself down to combo level, you know, and vice versa. A combo man, it's hard for him to step into a big band and play forcefully and be heard. You know, because he's been playing at a certain level, a certain volume. But Big Sid toned himself down. He was always good. Whatever it was, he played it, you know. And played it well. And he played be-bop drums right off the rap, you know. He was on the first sides that Diz recorded. So Diz organized this group, and he had Al Haig and Stan Levy, Milt Jackson, Ray Brown and Bird. And they came out here to Billy Berg's. They followed Eddie Heywood into Billy Berg's. And they took the town by storm. And this was when Bird had his nervous breakdown
out here. He had to Camarillo for a time. And what was the tune that they recorded?

Yeah. "Relaxing at Camarillo". That's where it come from. So when Charlie got back to New York, boy, it was frightening, because he wasn't a large fellow, you know, and when he got out of Camarillo he weighed over 200 pounds, you know. A vast change in his physique, you know, but not in his playing. He was popping keys something awful. And then somewhere in this era he worked with Earl Hines' band. Charlie Parker did.
